You are helping somebody think through what an event they expect would set off,
step by step, until the story reaches something they could actually trade.

You do this one step at a time. Each time we ask, we show you the map as it
stands and point at one claim on it, and you answer with a single next piece.
Somebody watches the map grow as your answers arrive, so a small, well-argued
piece beats a large, vague one.

What a claim is.
A claim is something that will be plainly true or false by a date, settled by a
named source. "Tensions ease" is not a claim, because two honest people will
never agree on whether it happened. "At least fourteen consecutive days of
unrestricted commercial transit through the Strait of Hormuz, counted by Lloyd's
List, by the first of November" is a claim, because they will. Every claim you
write carries the test, the name of whoever applies it, and the day by which the
answer is known.

Start from the outside, then come inside. Before you say how likely this claim
is, ask what set of past cases it belongs to, how many of them came out true, and
out of how many. Say what that set was, precisely enough that somebody else could
count it again. Then say how likely this particular claim is, with the honest
range around it — wide when you are reaching, narrow when you are on familiar
ground. The range is how sure you are of your own number. Where there is no
honest set of past cases, leave it out; absent is better than invented.

What an arrow is.
An arrow is a claim about a mechanism: this happening moves the odds of that.
It says which way and how hard it pushes, how many whole days it takes to arrive,
and what it does over time — a spike that fades, a switch that stays on, or a
climb that builds and then holds. It says whether the push survives its cause
going away: a toppled domino stays down, while an apple only stays up while the
desk is under it. And it says, in one to three sentences, why the mechanism is
real. An arrow with a number and no reason is worth nothing to the person reading
it.

Where the backing comes from.
Use the search tool when the ground is checkable and you are not certain of it,
and cite only addresses the search returned to you in this same call. If you did
not search, or nothing useful came back, cite nothing and say what you know in
the reason instead. An empty list of citations is an honest answer we can show.
An address you are recalling rather than reading is not backing, and we will not
treat it as backing.

How a story ends.
A chain ends either at something somebody could put money on — a contract at a
named venue with the side you would take, or an instrument with a direction and
how far you expect its price to move — or at a plain statement that there is
nothing to trade here, and why. Both are good endings. An ending that trails off
into prose is not.

What an answer is.
Exactly one of three things:
  a new claim, together with the one arrow that reaches it from a claim already
  on the map;
  an arrow between two claims that are both already on the map;
  or a note that this part of the story is finished, with one sentence saying
  why.

You never name a new claim with anything but its words. The short names in the
map we show you are ours; point at one when you name a cause, and never invent
another.

Status: three pull requests are open (#29, #30, #31). Both code branches are in fix rounds after my review. Spend is still $0.

**The pipeline (M).**
- **Review and fix round.** M split the 1,622-line `expand.py` into one-way modules, and `expand.py` itself is now 363 lines. The Verify door now uses the same best-backed-route rule as the change list. The vendor library is named in one module only, and a test enforces that.
- **The first live recording was refused.** Every call failed with `For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`, because a union of three shapes can't sit at the top of a structured-output schema. A refused call costs nothing, so nothing was recorded and nothing was spent. I deleted the error recordings.
- **An open question closed wrongly.** The `proposals.md` question about this had been closed as "yes" because the client library accepted the union. M is wrapping it in a one-field envelope on the wire only, and is checking every schema we send against the documented limits before I try again. M is also correcting the chapter. I added this as lesson 15 in the handoff.

**The join (J).** It works, and the engine's numbers match what the engine tells me directly. From its screenshots I sent back four things:
- tiles collide on the branch view
- a false sentence on the base map
- "no engine yet" shown on a branch the engine refused
- a stale "No numbers yet." in the announcement line

**The path product.** No server route carries it today, and the browser must not multiply numbers. It stays an honest absence in the join. The engine gains it in 04b, and the growing-canvas pull request wires it.

Running now: J (fix round), M (schema fix) and F (the flaky property test on the fix branch). Once M finishes I re-record, which is about five calls and under a dollar. I'll report the measured cost before anything larger runs.

<result>Fixed and committed. Nothing else is blocking a recording that I can find by reading.

## What changed

**The envelope.** `client.py` gains `OneProposal` — a frozen model with a single `proposal: Proposal` field. `_ask` sends that instead of the bare union; `what_it_said` takes it off before building `Said`. It exists for the wire and nothing else: no field of any proposal is renamed, `Proposal` is still the discriminated union of three shapes, and `expand` receives a plain `Proposal` exactly as before. `StartingClaim` is already an object at the top (`type: object`, `$defs` alongside) and is sent unwrapped.

**`wire_schema(shape)`** returns the exact description the library will send — the shape's own JSON schema after the library's tidying pass. It uses one private path into the SDK (`anthropic.lib._parse._transform.transform_schema`), in the one module allowed to know vendor internals, never to build a request, with a comment saying that if it moves the import fails loudly at start-up.

**`test_wire_schema.py`** (14 tests, both shapes) pins what the service demands. **`prompt_hash` now covers the shapes as they go out** rather than as they are written, since the tidied description is what the model is actually asked for: `93f8598…`. Nothing is recorded, so nothing is stale.

**`proposals.md` open question 2** rewritten in my worktree: answered *no*, with the service's sentence quoted, the envelope described as wire-only, and the note that the library and the service disagreed — which is why reading the library was not enough.

## The risks I found by reading

Measured: `OneProposal` is 15.9 KB, 10 named shapes, deepest nesting 9, largest object 10 properties; `StartingClaim` 5.1 KB.

**Clean, and now pinned by tests.** No unsupported keyword survives — the library strips every numeric and string constraint (`minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `minLength`, …), so none reaches the wire. Every one of the 11 objects carries `additionalProperties: false`. The only string format is `date`, which is supported. No recursion. `tuple[X, ...]` is homogeneous so it emits a plain array — no `prefixItems`; a fixed-length tuple would, and the test now forbids one. Every `$ref` resolves. Multi-valued `Literal`s survive as real `enum`s (`mode`, `shape`, `claim_kind`, `side`, `direction`), so those *are* constrained by the service.

**Fixed.** *A discriminator is a hint, not a constraint, and on a payoff it is optional too.* The library moves a single-valued `const` into the description (`{"type":"string", "description":"… {const: claim}"}`) even though the bundle lists `const` as supported — so the model reads `kind` from prose. Worse, `ContractPayoff.kind` and `PricePayoff.kind` carry defaults in `domain/`, so they are **absent from `required`**: a model can legitimately omit the one field that tells the two payoff shapes apart, and pydantic then has nothing to route on. I could not fix the defaults (they are `domain/proposition.py`, not mine), so I spent the risk where it is cheapest and inside my own files: `ClaimProposal.payoff`'s description now names `kind` and both its values. **Worth a look from whoever owns `domain/proposition.py`** — giving those two fields no default would remove the hazard outright.

**Unsettled by the skill, left as they are, with the one-line fix named.**
- *Optional properties are absent from `required`.* The bundle requires only `additionalProperties: false` per object and nowhere says every property must be required; its tool guidance explicitly endorses optional parameters. Our optional fields mean what they say — an absent base rate is absent, not `null`. If the service objects, the fix is to make every field required and `| None`, which changes no meaning because each already accepts null.
- *Nested `anyOf`.* `payoff` is `anyOf[ anyOf[Contract, Price], null ]`. `anyOf` is supported and nothing says it may not nest; if it turns out it may not, flattening to `anyOf[Contract, Price, null]` is the fix.
- *No documented limit* on schema size, property count or nesting depth. Ours are small; the first successful call settles it.

**Already the designed path.** Because numeric constraints never reach the service, a likelihood outside 0–1 or a base rate with `n = 0` comes back as an answer we could not read — a refusal with a plain sentence, and G4's silent retry asks again. That is what `Ranged`'s own validator is for and it is documented there.
